title: Death transformed into joy for the saints
english: In earlier times the deaths of the saints were adorned with lamentation and tears. Joseph wept bitterly for Jacob when he was dead, and the Jews mourned the death of Moses with no small grief. They honored Samuel too with many tears. But now we leap for joy at the deaths of the holy ones. For after the cross, the nature of sorrowful things has been changed. No longer do we escort the deaths of the saints with dirges, but we dance with inspired choirs around their tombs. For death is sleep for the righteous—or rather, a departure to a better life. That is why martyrs leap for joy as they are being slain. The longing for the more blessed life makes the pain of slaughter dead. The martyr does not see the dangers but the crowns; he does not shudder at the blows but counts the prizes; he does not look at the executioners scourging him below, but imagines the angels praising him above; he does not consider the temporary nature of the dangers, but the eternity of the rewards. Even now among us they enjoy a bright earnest, applauded by the inspired praises of all, and netting countless multitudes from their tombs. This is what the noble Barlaam has accomplished today. For the martial trumpet of the martyr has sounded, and it has gathered the soldiers of piety, as you see. The athlete of Christ, now laid out, has been proclaimed, and he has stirred up the assembly of the Church. And as the Master of the faithful said, “Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live” (John 11:25). The noble Barlaam has died, and he gathers festal assemblies; he has been consumed in the tomb, yet he summons us to a banquet. Now is the time for us to cry out, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). Today a rustic is our unconquerable teacher of piety—a man whom the tyrant dragged off as easy prey, but after testing him found an unconquerable soldier; a man he laughed at for his mangled speech, but shuddered at when he showed angelic youthful vigor. For his manner did not share in the broken speech of his tongue's instrument, nor was his reasoning seen limping along with his syllables. Rather, he was a second Paul, saying with Paul, “Even if I am untrained in speech, I am not in knowledge” (2 Corinthians 11:6). The scourging executioners grew numb, but the martyr was found more vigorous. The hands of those who flayed him were weakened, but the reasoning of the one being flayed was not bent. The whips loosened the harmonies of his sinews, but the tension of his faith was tightened all the more. His sides were dug into and worn away, but the philosophy of his spirit was in full bloom. Most of his flesh had been put to death, yet he flourished as one who had not yet begun the contests. For when love of piety takes hold of the soul in advance, every form of warfare becomes laughable to it, and all those who flay it for the sake of the beloved give it pleasure rather than pain. The longing of the apostles bears witness to me, making the whips they once received from the Jews delightful. For they went, it says, rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to be dishonored for his name (Acts 5:41). Such is the soldier we praise today. He considered tortures a joy, and thought he was being struck with roses by the whips. He fled the outrages of impiety as though they were arrows, and reckoned the judge’s fury a shadow of smoke. He laughed at the raging ranks of bodyguards, and danced among the dangers as though they were crowns. He rejoiced in the blows as though they were honors, and leaped for joy at the more severe punishments as though they were brighter prizes. He spat at drawn swords, and received the hands of the executioners as though they were softer than wax. He embraced the torturer’s wood as a saving wood, and delighted in the locks of the prison as though they were meadows. He took pleasure in the inventions of tortures as though they were varieties of flowers, and he possessed a right hand stronger than fire—the final device that his enemies brought against him.
orientation: Basil opens his homily on the martyr Barlaam by contrasting the old mourning of the dead with the Christian joy that now surrounds the deaths of the saints, since death is a passage to better life.

title: The hand as altar and the fire's defeat
english: They lit an altar for a drink offering to the demons, brought the martyr and stood him beside it, and ordered him to stretch his right hand out over the altar with the palm turned upward. They used the hand as a bronze altar, wickedly placing burning incense in it. For they hoped that the hand would be wrestled down by the force of the fire and would quickly be compelled to drop the incense onto the altar. What a tangled trick of the impious! “Since,” they say, “we have not bent his resolve with countless wounds, let us at least bend the hand of this stubborn wrestler in the fire. Since we have not shaken his soul with various devices, let us at least bring his right hand to the fire and make it waver.” But the wretches did not profit even from this hope. The fire gnawed through the hand, but the hand remained, bearing the flame as though it were ash. It did not turn its back to the attacking fire like a deserter, but stood unshaken, proving itself best against the fire, and giving the martyr the words of the Prophet to speak: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Psalm 18:34; Psalm 17:35 LXX). Fire grappled with a hand, and the fire was found to bear the marks of defeat. A wrestling match was joined between the fire and the martyr’s right hand, but the victory of the right hand’s wrestling moves was something new: the fire fell through the middle of the hand, while the hand remained stretched out for the contest. O hand more stubborn than fire! O hand that never learned to bend to fire! O fire that was taught to be defeated by a hand! Iron yields to the tyranny of fire and is softened. Bronze gives way to the power of fire. Even the resistance of stones, as we know, is overcome by it. But the force of fire that overpowers everything did not bend the martyr’s stretched-out right hand, even as it burned it. Fittingly the martyr might cry out to the Master: “You held my right hand, and in your counsel you guided me, and with glory you received me” (Psalm 73:24; Psalm 72:24 LXX). What shall I call you, noble soldier of Christ? Shall I call you a statue? I fall far short of your endurance. For fire, receiving it, softens a statue, but it could not make your right hand appear to move. If I call you iron, I find that even this image falls short of your courage. For you alone persuaded the fire not to force a hand. You alone made your right hand an altar. You alone with a burning right hand struck the faces of the demons, and then with a charred hand you melted their heads along with it; now with that hand burned to ashes you blind their armies as you trample them. But why do I diminish the champion with childish stammering? Let us yield the hymn in his honor to more magnificent tongues. Let us summon the louder trumpets of the teachers for him. Rise up now for me, brilliant painters of athletic achievements. Magnify with your arts the mutilated image of the commander. Illuminate with the colors of your wisdom the crowned victor whom I have painted too dimly. May I depart defeated by your painting of the martyr’s feats. I rejoice today to be defeated by such a victory of your strength. Let me see the wrestling match of the hand against the fire painted by you more accurately. Let me see the wrestler drawn more brightly on your image. Let the demons weep, struck now too by the martyr’s feats in your work. Let the burning hand be shown again to them, victorious. Let Christ also, the umpire of the wrestling matches, be inscribed on the tablet—to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
orientation: Basil is describing the climax of Barlaam's martyrdom: the persecutors place burning incense in his outstretched right hand over a lit altar, hoping the fire will force him to drop it, but the hand remains unconquered.
